subsection: The musculoskeletal system as a system for response

notes.b: The musculoskeletal system is the framework of bones and joints together with the muscles that move it. Between them they let the body respond to a stimulus (a change in the surroundings) by moving.
points: The skeleton is the bones, together with the cartilage and ligaments that join them at joints (the places where two bones meet).
The skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons, which are the other part of the system.
Muscles provide the force, bones act as rigid levers, and joints are the pivots where movement happens, so a muscle pulling on a bone moves it at a joint.
The parts are only named here. There is more on the bones in "The axial skeleton" and "The appendicular skeleton", and on the joints and muscle pairs in "Muscles and joints".
The adult human skeleton has 206 bones, which are divided into two groups.
80 of these form the axial skeleton: the skull, vertebral column (backbone), ribs and sternum (breastbone), which make up the central axis of the body.
The other 126 form the appendicular skeleton: the pectoral girdle (shoulders), the pelvic girdle (hips) and the limbs attached to them.
notes.tip: If asked to name the components of the musculoskeletal system, give bones, cartilage, ligaments, joints, skeletal muscles and tendons.

notes.b: Bones look like lifeless sticks, but bone is a living tissue made of cells. Its structure explains why it is both hard and tough.
points: Bone is a living connective tissue, which means a tissue that supports and holds the body together.
Bone cells lie in a hard matrix (the material around the cells) of calcium phosphate, which gives bone its hardness and resists compression (being squashed).
Collagen fibres in the matrix give bone some flexibility and resist bending and snapping, so bone is not brittle like chalk.
Bone has a blood supply and nerves, can grow and repair itself, and changes shape slowly in response to the forces put on it.

notes.b: The skeleton does much more than hold us up. It has five functions, and each one can be illustrated with an example.
points: Support: the skeleton is a rigid framework that holds the body up, gives it its shape and supports soft organs. The vertebral column supports the head and trunk, and the leg bones carry the body's weight.

Protection: bones surround delicate organs so that knocks do not damage them. The skull protects the brain, the ribs and sternum protect the heart and lungs, the vertebrae protect the spinal cord, and the pelvic girdle protects the bladder and reproductive organs.
Movement: bones provide attachment points for muscles and act as levers that the muscles pull on, moving the body at joints.
Making blood cells: red bone marrow, found in spongy bone (the light, honeycomb-like bone), makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
In adults, red marrow is mainly in the flat bones (skull, ribs, sternum, vertebrae and pelvis) and in the ends of long bones such as the femur (thigh bone) and humerus (upper arm bone).
Yellow marrow fills the hollow shafts of long bones and stores fat.
Storing minerals: bone stores calcium and phosphate.

When blood calcium falls, calcium is released from bone under the control of parathyroid hormone, which helps keep blood calcium constant. This matters because nerves and muscles need calcium to work. There is more on this in "Glands, locations and hormones".
notes.tip: Exams ask you to state the functions of the skeleton with an example of each, so always pair a function with a named bone and organ, such as the skull protecting the brain.

notes.b: The body has three types of muscle, and they differ in where they are, whether you can control them, how they look and how they contract. Only one of them belongs to the musculoskeletal system.
points: Skeletal muscle is attached to bones by tendons and is the only muscle type in the musculoskeletal system. It is under voluntary (conscious) control as well as reflex control, and its cells look striped (striated) under the microscope.
Skeletal muscle contracts quickly and powerfully but tires (fatigues), which is why you cannot keep sprinting indefinitely.
Smooth muscle is found in the walls of the gut, blood vessels, bladder and uterus. It is involuntary (not under conscious control) and not striped.
Smooth muscle contracts slowly and can stay contracted for a long time, as in peristalsis (the waves of squeezing that push food along the gut).

Cardiac muscle is found only in the wall of the heart. It is involuntary and striped, and it contracts rhythmically throughout life without tiring. There is more on the heart in "The Circulatory System and Blood".
notes.tip: You may be asked to name the three types of muscle and give a location and one feature of each. Remember that only skeletal muscle is part of the musculoskeletal system.

notes.b: A skeletal muscle is the effector that carries out a response, in the same way as the other effectors (the parts that act on a nerve message) such as glands. There is more on this in "Structures and systems for response". To see how it works, start with what it is made of.
points: A skeletal muscle is made of bundles of long cells called muscle fibres.
Each fibre contains many nuclei and many mitochondria, so it has plenty of control and plenty of energy supply for contraction.
Each fibre is packed with two kinds of protein filament: thin filaments of actin and thick filaments of myosin.
The filaments are arranged in repeating units that give the striped appearance of skeletal muscle.

notes.h: How a nerve message makes a skeletal muscle contract
notes.b: A skeletal muscle never contracts on its own. It contracts only when it is stimulated by a motor neuron (a nerve cell that carries impulses to a muscle), and the contraction follows a fixed sequence.
points: 1. Skeletal muscle contracts only when it is stimulated by a motor neuron. A voluntary movement starts in the brain; a reflex movement starts in the spinal cord. There is more on this in "The reflex action".
2. Impulses travel along the motor neuron to its ending on the muscle fibre, a synapse (a gap between nerve and target) called the neuromuscular junction.
3. At the neuromuscular junction the neurotransmitter (chemical messenger) acetylcholine is released, crosses the gap and binds to receptors on the muscle fibre, starting an impulse in the fibre.
4. The impulse causes calcium ions (Ca²⁺) to be released from stores inside the fibre.
5. The calcium allows myosin filaments to attach to actin filaments and pull them inwards, so the filaments slide past each other and the fibre shortens.
6. Energy for this comes from ATP, the energy carrier of the cell, which is made in the many mitochondria by respiration.
notes.tip: To explain how a skeletal muscle acts as an effector, take the sequence in order: motor neuron, neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine, calcium release, actin and myosin sliding, energy from ATP.

notes.h: Relaxing, pulling and controlling the strength of a response
notes.b: Contraction is only half the story. The muscle must also relax, and the nervous system must be able to vary how hard the muscle pulls.
points: When the impulses stop, calcium is pumped back into its stores, the filaments detach and the muscle relaxes.
A relaxed muscle does not lengthen by itself: it is pulled back to its full length by an opposing muscle, which is why muscles work in pairs. There is more on this in "Muscles and joints".
A muscle can only pull by contracting; it can never push.
The force is passed through a tendon to a bone, which moves at a joint. This movement is the response.
Strength of response: the more motor neurons that fire and the more muscle fibres that contract, the stronger the contraction, so movements can be gentle or forceful.
Muscle tone: a slight, continuous partial contraction of muscles holds the body's posture without conscious effort.

Diagram: a flow diagram of a voluntary response: brain, spinal cord, motor neuron, neuromuscular junction, skeletal muscle (contracts), tendon, bone moves at joint. Also a sketch of a skeletal muscle cut open to show bundles of muscle fibres, with one fibre enlarged to show actin and myosin filaments, all labelled.
notes.tip: Never say a muscle pushes, and never say a relaxed muscle lengthens itself: its opposing muscle pulls it back. Exams ask why muscles work in pairs.

notes.b: Because skeletal muscle is attached to bones, the system produces a wide range of responses, from obvious movements to constant small adjustments you never notice.
points: Movement of the whole body (locomotion: walking, running, swimming) to find food, escape danger or move to better conditions.
Movement of parts of the body, such as grasping or turning the head towards a sound.
Maintaining posture and balance: muscles of the back, neck and legs make constant small adjustments, in response to information from receptors, to keep the body upright.
Breathing: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles (the muscles between the ribs) move the ribs. There is more on this in "Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism".
Speech, facial expression, chewing and swallowing all depend on skeletal muscle.
Shivering: rapid involuntary contractions that release heat when the body is cold.

notes.h: How the system depends on other systems
notes.b: Muscles and bones cannot respond alone. They depend on other body systems to start the contraction, to supply fuel and to prepare them for action.
points: Nervous system: every contraction of a skeletal muscle is started by a motor neuron.
Receptors in muscles and joints send information back to the brain about the position of the limbs, so that movements can be coordinated.
Circulatory and breathing systems: active muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration, and must remove more carbon dioxide and heat, so heart rate and breathing rate rise during exercise.
When oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough, muscle fibres respire anaerobically (without oxygen), producing lactic acid and much less ATP, and soon tire (fatigue).
The lactic acid is removed afterwards, when oxygen is available again; this is one reason breathing stays fast after exercise. There is more on this in "Respiration".
Endocrine system: adrenaline (a hormone) increases blood flow to skeletal muscles and raises blood glucose, preparing them for action.
Health: regular weight-bearing exercise, such as walking or running, strengthens bones and muscles.
A diet with enough protein (for muscle), calcium and vitamin D (for bone) supports the system.
notes.tip: Lactic acid is not the only cause of fatigue, so do not say it is. Say that anaerobic respiration gives much less ATP and produces lactic acid.

keyTerms.definition: The skeleton together with the skeletal muscles and tendons that move it.
The skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum, which form the central axis of the body.
The pectoral and pelvic girdles and the bones of the limbs attached to them.
Striped muscle attached to bones by tendons, under voluntary and reflex control, which contracts quickly and tires.
Involuntary, unstriped muscle in the walls of the gut, blood vessels, bladder and uterus, which contracts slowly.
Involuntary, striped muscle found only in the heart wall, which contracts rhythmically without tiring.
A long muscle cell containing many nuclei and mitochondria and packed with actin and myosin filaments.
The synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fibre, where acetylcholine is released.
A slight, continuous partial contraction of muscles that holds the body's posture without conscious effort.

questions.prompt: Give three functions of the human skeleton, with an example of each.
questions.model: Support: the skeleton is a rigid framework that holds the body up and supports soft organs; the leg bones carry the body's weight. Protection: the skull protects the brain, and the vertebrae protect the spinal cord. Movement: bones provide attachment points for muscles and act as levers that the muscles pull on, moving the body at joints, for example the humerus moves the forearm at the elbow.

questions.prompt: Explain how the musculoskeletal system acts as the effector in a response to a stimulus.
questions.model: A motor neuron stimulates the skeletal muscle, starting a voluntary or reflex response. At the neuromuscular junction, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine is released, crosses the gap and binds to receptors on the muscle fibre, starting an impulse in the fibre. The impulse releases calcium ions inside the fibre. The calcium allows myosin filaments to attach to actin filaments and pull them so the fibre shortens; ATP supplies the energy. The muscle can only pull, and its contraction is passed through a tendon to a bone, which moves at a joint.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle in terms of location, control and appearance.
questions.model: Skeletal muscle is attached to bones by tendons, for example in the limbs. It is under voluntary as well as reflex control, and its cells look striped under the microscope. Smooth muscle is found in the walls of the gut, blood vessels, bladder and uterus. It is involuntary, meaning it is not under conscious control, and its cells are not striped.
